title: ASS1-derived argininosuccinate promotes purine nucleoside synthesis in B cell acute lymphoblastic leukaemia
abstract: Metabolic remodelling underlies tumour progression. However, how metabolites act as signalling molecules to support cancer cell proliferation remains unclear. Here we show that argininosuccinate (ASA), a key intermediate of the urea cycle, promotes purine nucleoside biosynthesis in tyrosine kinase-driven haematological malignancies. Mechanistically, BCR–ABL phosphorylates argininosuccinate synthase 1 (ASS1), which increases ASA production from citrulline. ASA directly binds cytosolic 5′-nucleotidase II (NT5C2) and enhances its nucleosidase activity. The resulting purine nucleosides serve as a carbon source for glycolysis and the tricarboxylic acid cycle, which supports leukaemia cell proliferation under glucose-replete conditions. Loss of ASS1 or NT5C2 disrupts central carbon metabolism and inhibits leukaemia progression in vivo, which can be rescued with inosine or adenosine supplementation. Collectively, our findings uncover an ASA–NT5C2 signalling axis linking urea cycle dysregulation to purine metabolism, and identify purine nucleosides as a carbon source in tyrosine kinase-driven haematological malignancies.

title: Increasing cytosolic NADPH to mimic exercise
abstract: In this issue of Nature Metabolism, Wu et al. reveal that cytosolic NADPH, a pentose phosphate pathway metabolite, drives a physiological cardiac hypertrophic response that is protective against heart attack injury and can be raised by a candidate spermidine derivative.

title: Pentose phosphate pathway-derived NADPH facilitates physiological hypertrophy and alleviates ischemia–reperfusion injury in the heart
abstract: Exercise promotes physiological cardiomyocyte growth and protects against ischaemia–reperfusion (IR) injury in the heart. The molecular mechanism by which exercise benefits cardiac metabolism and function remains largely unknown. Here, using a genetically encoded fluorescent sensor, we show that exercise increases cytosolic, but not mitochondrial, NADPH levels in cardiomyocytes. This effect is mediated by activation of the pentose phosphate pathway (PPP). Inhibition of PPP activity or depletion of cytosolic NADPH attenuates exercise-induced heart hypertrophy in mice. We observe that NADPH promotes cardiomyocyte growth by inhibiting HDAC3/C/EBPβ pathways. Moreover, exercise-activated PPP/NADPH pathway suppresses acute IR injury and preserves heart function 4 weeks after IR. Among 310 tested Tibetan compounds, the spermidine derivative lyciumspermidine-0527 directly activates the rate-limiting PPP enzyme glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase, elevates intracellular NADPH levels and alleviates IR injury. Altogether, these results show that PPP-derived NADPH is a critical metabolic checkpoint that regulates exercise-induced physiological cardiomyocyte growth and protects against IR-induced heart injury.

ALKBH5 activates creatine-driven thermogenesis by stabilizing CKB mRNA in response to cold
abstract: Non-shivering thermogenesis contributes to increased energy expenditure and can be a potential therapy to combat obesity. Here we show that the adipose tissue N 6 -methyladenosine (m 6 A) demethylase ALKBH5 responds to cold and adrenergic stimulation to induce non-shivering thermogenesis independent of UCP1. Fat-specific Alkbh5 knockout reduces thermogenic capacity, increases susceptibility to obesity and disrupts glucose homoeostasis in both male and female mice. Conversely, Alkbh5 overexpression in thermogenic fat increases energy expenditure and improves systemic metabolism. Furthermore, fat ALKBH5 expression inversely correlates with obesity in humans. Mechanistically, ALKBH5 is transcriptionally induced by the cAMP/PKA/CREB pathway in response to thermogenic stimuli. ALKBH5 demethylates m 6 A on CKB mRNA and prevents its degradation mediated by YTHDF2, thereby enhancing creatine metabolism-mediated thermogenesis in both wild-type and Ucp1 -knockout mice. These findings suggest that ALKBH5 transduces thermogenic signalling towards creatine-driven thermogenesis, serving as a potential target for the treatment of obesity.

title: Paediatric proteomic signatures of cardiometabolic disease-associated traits predict adult disease outcomes
abstract: While the earliest pathological signs of cardiovascular–kidney–metabolic disease (CKMD) emerge before age 20, current adult-based risk thresholds fail to identify a substantial fraction of children at high risk. With increasing childhood obesity, early, sensitive detection of CKMD risk is critical to timely intervention. We linked 25 CKMD phenotypes spanning liver, adipose, vascular and dysglycaemia traits to the circulating proteome in 273 Hispanic or Latino children and adolescents (13.1 ± 2.7 years; 53% female). Here we show that proteome signatures of CKMD in children are strongly associated with clinical CKMD outcomes in adults. In 685 adults from the same community and 28,256 adults from UK Biobank, we observe high concordance between the paediatric and adult CKMD phenotype–proteome relationships, related to pancreatic beta-cell health and insulin sensitivity, liver homeostasis, inflammation and cholesterol metabolism. Many proteins linked to paediatric CKMD were modifiable with glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist therapy in adults and are linked to genetic liability to CKMD. These findings support an early origin of CKMD disease liability embedded in the human proteome in children, underscoring the value of precision prevention to forestall metabolic disease long before its clinical manifestation.

title: Pick and choose
abstract: Great science comes in all shapes and sizes. Choosing the most suitable article type is key to managing the expectations of readers, editors and reviewers alike.

title: Childhood proteomic signatures that predict adult cardiometabolic disease
abstract: Early signs of cardiovascular–kidney–metabolic disease (CKMD) emerge before 20 years of age, but methods to identify CKMD risk in children are limited. We identified a proteomic and phenotypic signature of CKMD in children that is strongly associated with the development and clinical outcomes of CKMD in adulthood.

title: Argininosuccinate signalling drives carbon replenishment in B cell acute lymphoblastic leukaemia
abstract: Argininosuccinate synthase 1 (ASS1) phosphorylation is elevated in samples from patients with B cell acute lymphoblastic leukaemia and in leukaemic cells. As ASS1-derived argininosuccinate was found to activate cytosolic NT5C2 to promote purine nucleoside biosynthesis and replenish cellular carbon sources, ASS1 and NT5C2 are potential therapeutic targets for tyrosine kinase-driven haematological malignancies.

title: Cagrilintide and retatrutide combination therapy enhances weight loss and metabolic outcomes in obese male rats
abstract: Peptide multi-receptor agonists have advanced obesity treatment, yet challenges remain in achieving maximal weight loss and metabolic control, especially in patients with obesity and type 2 diabetes. Here we demonstrate enhanced metabolic benefits of a combination therapy with retatrutide, a unimolecular GLP-1R/GIPR/GCGR tri-agonist, and cagrilintide, an AMLNR/CALCR co-agonist, in diet-induced obese male rats. Daily co-administration produces dose-dependent reductions in body weight and food intake that exceed both equimolar monotherapies and matched-dose comparator combinations incorporating semaglutide or tirzepatide. The combination therapy also improves circulating markers of metabolic health, including cholesterol, triglycerides and insulin levels. Pair-feeding and weight-matching studies reveal that the enhanced weight loss cannot be explained by reduced food intake alone and enable discrimination between weight-loss-dependent and drug-specific molecular responses. Plasma proteomic profiling highlights enrichment of bioenergetic processes with the combination therapy, whereas brain transcriptomic profiling identifies convergent central neuronal programmes linked to energy balance regulation. Collectively, our preclinical findings support five-receptor polypharmacology as a strategy for efficaciously lowering body weight and provide guidance for the design of next-generation unimolecular multi-receptor agonists.

title: The high price of ‘free’ cysteine
abstract: Cells depend on cysteine, but excess free cysteine comes at a price. Nakamura et al. show that excess cysteine disrupts mitochondrial iron homeostasis, which drives a distinct iron-dependent cell death, revealing why cells rapidly channel cysteine into glutathione synthesis.

title: Cysteine excess triggers a mitochondrial iron-dependent cell death
abstract: Thiol-containing metabolites are central to cellular redox homeostasis 1 . Among these, cysteine functions as a proteogenic amino acid, supports redox balance and iron–sulfur cluster biogenesis, and, when depleted, triggers ferroptosis 2 . Cells nevertheless maintain cysteine at low levels, reflecting its intrinsic toxicity, but the mechanisms by which excess cysteine causes cell death remain unclear 3 . Here we performed a genome-wide CRISPR screen and identified mitochondrial iron transporters as essential mediators of cysteine toxicity. Limiting mitochondrial iron availability suppresses cysteine-induced cell death and prevents impairment of iron–sulfur cluster proteins and respiration. Mechanistically, cysteine mobilizes iron from ferritin, expands the cytosolic iron pool and drives mitochondrial iron accumulation. Enhancing glutathione reductase activity specifically within mitochondria restores redox balance downstream of iron accumulation and protects cells by maintaining iron–sulfur cluster integrity. Our findings suggest that maintaining low cysteine levels safeguards mitochondrial iron homeostasis, and that excess cysteine triggers a distinct mitochondrial iron-dependent cell death under conditions of thiol imbalance.

Effects of time-restricted eating in early-stage Huntington’s disease: a pilot study
abstract: Time-restricted eating (TRE) has shown neuroprotective potential in preclinical models of Huntington’s disease (HD) but has not been tested clinically. Here, we report the results of a 12-week open-label pilot trial ( NCT06490367 ) of 8-h TRE, alongside standard-of-care diet and activity recommendations, in 20 individuals with early-stage HD. We show that TRE is feasible, well tolerated and associated with favourable changes in clinical measures of HD and plasma neurofilament light levels. Overall, these results support the need for further investigation of TRE as a potential lifestyle intervention in HD.

title: Meal timing as medicine: clinical evidence for intermittent fasting in Huntington’s disease
abstract: In a 12-week pilot study, 20 people with early-stage Huntington’s disease restricted their eating to a daily 6–8-h window. The intervention was feasible and well-tolerated, and exploratory analyses suggested improvements in clinical measures, levels of plasma neurofilament light (a biomarker of neurodegeneration) and cellular bioenergetics.

title: mRNA methylation safeguards pancreatic α-cell identity against cellular plasticity
abstract: The epitranscriptomic mRNA modification N6-methyladenosine (m6A) helps to maintain the functional identity of pancreatic α-cells. Deletion of the m6A writer METTL14 impairs amino acid-stimulated glucagon secretion, destabilizes the α-cell state and promotes plasticity towards immature, insulin-secreting β-cell-like fates.

title: m6A mRNA methylation regulates pancreatic α-cell plasticity
abstract: Pancreatic α-cells are central regulators of glucose and amino acid homeostasis, yet the mechanisms that preserve α-cell identity and function remain incompletely understood. N 6 -methyladenosine (m 6 A) is a widespread mRNA modification that is essential for β-cell biology and pancreatic endocrine differentiation. Here we show that m 6 A is a key regulator of α-cell function and plasticity. In α-cells, metabolic cues that stimulate glucagon secretion such as L -arginine increase METTL3, METTL14 and m 6 A levels. Loss of m 6 A impairs amino acid-stimulated glucagon secretion, disrupts α-cell identity programmes and induces metabolic rewiring. In mice, α-cell-specific Mettl14 deletion reduces α-cell mass, increases β-cell mass and promotes α-to-β-cell conversion, accompanied by the emergence of late β-like states with features of incomplete maturation. Mechanistically, m 6 A-eCLIP identifies Yy1 as a direct m 6 A-sensitive target, and elevated YY1 links m 6 A loss to signalling rewiring and erosion of α-cell identity. These findings identify m 6 A as a central regulator of α-cell state and reveal an epitranscriptomic mechanism controlling endocrine cell plasticity.

title: Gut microbiome maturation in early childhood interacts with host genetics to predict type 1 diabetes risk
abstract: Prospective evidence linking early-life microbiome development and host genetics with type 1 diabetes (T1D) risk is limited. Here, we describe how gut microbiome maturation and host genetics influence T1D risk in the TEDDY study. We analysed 12,151 longitudinal metagenomes and host genetic data from 887 children at high genetic risk for T1D followed for up to 6 years. We identify three microbiome maturational patterns: Early Matured, Late Matured and Early Plateaued, driven primarily by non-linear changes in species from the Bifidobacterium and Ruminococcus genera. The Early Matured pattern is enriched in galactose metabolism and exhibits higher production of aromatic amino acids and B-group vitamins at early follow-ups, whereas the Early Plateaued pattern has increased microbial production of branched-chain amino acids. Notably, the Early Plateaued pattern is associated with a threefold elevated risk of T1D, whereas other patterns are not associated with T1D risk. Furthermore, we find that host genetic variants related to antimicrobial and antiviral immune responses modify the association between the Late Matured pattern and T1D risk. These findings highlight the role of early microbial exposures and host genetics in T1D susceptibility.

Size-dependent plastic exposure disrupts macrophage function and tissue-specific metabolism
abstract: Plastic pollution is an emerging yet understudied environmental risk to the immune system. Once ingested, microplastic and nanoplastic particles (MNPs) can translocate from the gut to internal organs 1 , 2 , 3 , with macrophages serving as primary targets 4 . Kupffer cells (KCs), the liver-resident macrophages, have a central role in immune surveillance and metabolism 5 , yet their response to MNPs remains unclear. Here we identify KCs as the primary hepatic reservoir for MNPs in young male mice. Chronic plastic exposure over 12 weeks alters their transcriptional profile, impairs phagocytic function and is associated with metabolic dysregulation of hepatocytes. Microplastics, but not nanoplastics, reduce KC-mediated clearance of circulating cells. Under diet-induced obesity, microplastics exacerbate hepatic lipid accumulation, while nanoplastics alter systemic glucose metabolism and energy expenditure. These findings demonstrate that chronic MNP exposure disrupts macrophage function in a size-dependent manner, with subsequent distinct consequences for liver and systemic metabolism.

title: MRMhub: a scalable data-processing framework for large-scale targeted metabolomics
Senolytics dasatinib and quercetin in metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis: a proof-of-principle randomized, controlled trial
abstract: Cellular senescence plays an important role in hepatic inflammation and fibrosis 1 , 2 , 3 . However, whether senescence represents a potential therapeutic target in humans with metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH) remains unexplored. Here we report the results of a phase-2, double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled trial of intermittent senolytic therapy with dasatinib plus quercetin (D + Q) in participants with fibrotic MASH. Thirty-one participants (median age 56 years; 76% male; 58% with type 2 diabetes) were randomized (1:1) to receive D + Q (dasatinib 100 mg per day plus quercetin 1,000 mg per day) or placebo for three consecutive days per week over 3 weeks, repeated across three 7-week cycles. The primary endpoint, ≥1 stage fibrosis improvement without MASH worsening on paired liver biopsies, is achieved in 47% of D + Q-treated participants versus 7% with placebo ( P = 0.02). MASH resolution occurs more frequently with D + Q than placebo (53% versus 7%; P = 0.02), with a greater reduction in NAFLD Activity Score (−1.43 ± 1.22 versus −0.39 ± 0.77; P = 0.012). Single-nucleus RNA sequencing demonstrates decreased senescence and fibrotic gene signatures and reduced fibrogenic cell populations in the D + Q group. Although adverse events are more frequent in the D + Q group (82% versus 43%), these are all self-limiting. Overall, this proof-of-principle trial supports the need for future trials of senolytic therapy in fibrotic MASH. ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT05506488 .

title: Maternal obesity imprints methylation marks in oocytes to drive intergenerational metabolic dysfunction
abstract: Maternal obesity predisposes offspring to metabolic disease, yet how oocytes transmit this risk remains unclear. Here, we show that maternal obesity induces locus-specific DNA methylation changes in oocytes to drive intergenerational metabolic dysfunction in a tissue-specific and sex-specific manner. Among these, a subset of metabolic genes, notably Hnf1α , Thra and Pdk4 , exhibited persistent intergenerational methylation and transcriptional dysregulation. Although these methylation marks were erased during embryogenesis, H3K36me2 enrichment was retained at the loci, suggesting a potential chromatin-associated cue for methylation re-establishment. Single-CpG analysis identified regulatory landmarks correlating with gene expression, and conserved hypermethylation of HNF1A and THRA was also detected in oocytes from women with obesity. Using methylation-edited mouse models, we further demonstrated that targeted oocyte hypermethylation at Hnf1α enhanced hepatic gluconeogenesis in offspring, whereas Pdk4 hypermethylation impaired glucose tolerance, both in a female-biased manner. Together, our findings provide direct causal evidence that germline methylation at defined loci can programme intergenerational metabolic dysfunction, highlighting the preconception period as a critical window for potential intervention in humans.

title: Metabolic and neural responses to ultraprocessed foods: a randomized, controlled, crossover study
abstract: Dietary patterns worldwide have shifted toward increased consumption of ultraprocessed foods (UPFs), which has been linked to higher disease burden. One proposed mechanism underlying both UPF consumption and metabolic disease is altered post-ingestive responses relative to nutritionally similar foods. Here we report the effects of food processing on post-ingestive metabolism and brain response in a randomized, crossover study involving 57 healthy-weight adults who consumed a nutritionally matched UPF or non-UPF meal. We show that despite being nutritionally similar, UPF meals evoke greater insulinaemic and energetic responses, with attenuated carbohydrate oxidation relative to non-UPF meals. Between-condition differences in peak carbohydrate oxidation are associated with striatal activation in response to food cues. We also find that although subjective food value does not differ between conditions, brain responses correlated with food valuation are positive for non-UPF but negative for UPF in the visual cortex and striatum. Overall, these findings suggest that food processing influences post-ingestive metabolic and neural responses through mechanisms beyond calories and macronutrients alone.

title: Ultraprocessed foods evoke distinct metabolic and neural responses
abstract: Ultraprocessed foods have been linked with various poor health outcomes. In our study, we characterize acute metabolic responses to these foods and investigate how our brains might encode food value, both nutritional and monetary.

title: l-Arginine inhibits NLRP3 inflammasome activation
abstract: Nutritional status and metabolic homeostasis are intricately associated with the inflammatory response. However, the direct mechanistic link between nutrition, metabolism and inflammation remains unclear. Here, we show that the amino acid l -arginine ( l -Arg) is a potent endogenous inhibitor of the NLRP3 inflammasome, a central component of the inflammatory signalling pathway. We show that l -Arg binds directly to the Asp31 site of the NLRP3 protein, blocking its interaction with the adaptor ASC and subsequent inflammasome assembly and activation. l -Arg supplementation inhibits the NLRP3 inflammasome activation in macrophages, while deprivation promotes it. Treatment with l -Arg in mice alleviates monosodium urate crystal-induced arthritis and aluminium-induced peritonitis. In addition, l -Arg supplementation alleviates neuroinflammation and motor deficits in mouse models of Parkinson’s disease, whereas l- Arg deprivation exacerbates pathology. In patients with Parkinson’s disease, l- Arg levels are reduced in serum. Our study establishes l- Arg supplementation as a promising therapeutic avenue for managing NLRP3-driven inflammatory pathologies.

title: Arginine inhibits a key innate immune signalling hub
abstract: The NLRP3 inflammasome has crucial roles in immunity and disease and is a key target for therapeutic efforts. In this issue of Nature Metabolism, Liu et al. show that l-arginine can inhibit inflammasome activation, highlighting the potential of dietary arginine supplementation as a treatment for NLRP3-related disease.

title: Author Correction: Brain regulation of gastric dysfunction induced by stress
Metabolic benefits of ketohexokinase inhibition in individuals with MASLD: a randomized placebo-controlled crossover trial
authors: Yvonne M. H. Op den Kamp-Bruls
abstract: High fructose consumption, particularly from sugar-sweetened beverages, contributes to cardiometabolic disease. Here we study the metabolic effects of 6-week pharmacological inhibition with PF-06835919 of ketohexokinase, the enzyme that catalyses the first committed step of fructose metabolism, in a randomized placebo-controlled crossover trial in 15 participants with metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease. The primary outcome was hepatic insulin sensitivity, measured by insulin-stimulated suppression of endogenous glucose production. Secondary outcomes included fat distribution, peripheral and adipose tissue insulin sensitivity, and fat oxidation. While PF-06835919 treatment did not affect body weight, it improved hepatic insulin sensitivity and reduced intrahepatic lipid and saturated fatty acid content. Besides these beneficial hepatic effects, PF-06835919 also improved insulin-stimulated glucose disposal, adipose tissue insulin sensitivity, adipose tissue distribution and nocturnal fat oxidation. These changes are accompanied by changes in very low-density lipoprotein particle size distribution and circulating hepatokines. These results show that inhibition of fructose metabolism has beneficial metabolic effects that extend beyond the organs that metabolize fructose. ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT05463575 .

title: Inhibiting fructose metabolism to treat fatty liver
abstract: In this issue of Nature Metabolism, Koene et al. present evidence that inhibiting fructose metabolism (using a ketohexokinase inhibitor) can improve hepatic steatosis and insulin resistance in individuals who are prediabetic with obesity and metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease, supporting further development and testing of fructose inhibitors in metabolic disease.

title: Systemic proteomic dynamics of acute exercise reveal genetic links to health and disease
abstract: Physical activity improves metabolic health, but the molecular responses that mediate its benefits are not fully characterized. Here we present a high-resolution, time-resolved proteomics atlas across plasma, saliva and urine from 25 healthy men in response to acute exercise. We find that exercise regulates more than 3,000 proteins through distinct, fluid-specific temporal dynamics. Network analysis uncovers coordinated remodelling of protein secretion, extracellular matrix and immune activation across body fluids. Replication in an independent cohort shows that many exercise-responsive plasma proteins exhibit consistent responses across age, sex and exercise modalities. Integration with human genome-wide association study data links secreted, exercise-responsive proteins to cardiometabolic diseases. Functional validation of genetically prioritized muscle-specific secreted proteins in Drosophila confirms their role in endurance, behaviour and metabolism. Overall, this open-access atlas ( https://cbmr.ku.dk/research/research-groups/deshmukh-group/shiny-apps/ ) provides a multifluid resource that complements existing exercise-omics efforts for defining molecular adaptations to exercise and for prioritizing candidate exerkines.

title: A multi-fluid exercise proteomic atlas reveals regulators of health and disease
abstract: A single bout of exercise triggers thousands of coordinated protein changes across blood, saliva and urine. By integrating tissue atlases, human genetics and in vivo functional validation, we present a multi-fluid resource that serves as a starting point for prioritizing robust candidate exercise-regulated proteins that might mediate the cardiometabolic health benefits of long-term exercise.

title: Genetic modulation of NAD(P)H homeostasis reveals distinct redox-coupled metabolic vulnerabilities
abstract: An elevated NADH/NAD + ratio (NADH-reductive stress) is a hallmark of mitochondrial dysfunction, yet how it drives pathologies ranging from primary mitochondrial disorders to ageing remains poorly understood 1 , 2 . Here, we show that mitochondrial respiratory chain inhibition in primary human fibroblasts induces NADH-reductive stress that coexists with profound NADPH depletion. Using the E scherichia coli soluble transhydrogenase ( Ec STH) 3 to model this redox coupling in cells with intact mitochondria, we demonstrate that perturbation of both NAD(H) and NADP(H) redox pairs elicits metabolomic and transcriptomic reprogramming, culminating in proliferation arrest with senescence features. Notably, normalizing the NADH/NAD + ratio alone while NADPH depletion persists fails to rescue proliferation in Ec STH-expressing primary human cells, unlike in transformed HeLa cells. Stable isotope tracing reveals that primary fibroblasts rely more on NADPH-driven reductive carboxylation than HeLa cells, explaining why NADH/NAD + normalization alone is insufficient for rescue. To test this NADPH dependency, we develop a constitutively active Staphylococcus aureus NAD kinase ( Sa NADK) that expands the mammalian NADP(H) pool. In fibroblasts, Sa NADK restores reductive carboxylation and de novo pyrimidine biosynthesis, and reverses proliferation arrest and senescence features. Furthermore, hepatic Sa NADK expression in aged male mice partially alleviates transcriptional signatures of inflammation and metabolic dysregulation. Together, these findings establish Ec STH and Sa NADK as xenotopic tools for dissecting NAD(P)H redox coupling and provide a framework for counteracting ageing-associated metabolic decline.

title: IRF7 signalling in tanycytes controls brain–body–immune response across the ovarian cycle
abstract: Sex-specific differences in metabolic and immune function are shaped by endocrine–immune interactions, yet the complexity of this relationship remains poorly understood. Here, we identify an immune cell-like state of tanycytes, an ependymoglial cell type lining the third ventricle that mediates brain–body communication 1 , 2 in both mice and humans. Using single-cell transcriptomics, we provide a high-resolution cellular map of the mouse and human mediobasal hypothalamus with cross-species comparison of tanycytes. We capture dynamic sex-, oestrous cycle- and high-fat diet-dependent transcriptomic changes in tanycytes, including a cyclic interferon response in tanycytes during the physiological oestrous cycle in female mice. We found that the oestrous cycle, with its changing hormonal milieu, especially oestradiol, affected the brain’s immune responses, characterized by the temporal and cyclic expression of interferon regulatory factor 7 ( Irf7 ) gene, as well as downstream interferon-stimulated genes such as Cxcl10 in tanycytes of female mice, which are associated with increased infiltration of leukocytes and cytokine responses. Irf7 expression in tanycytes of physiological males remained stable and markedly lower, suggesting a distinct immune activation pattern in the brains of cycling females. By targeting oestrogen and interferon signaling in tanycytes, we show that balanced, cyclic leukocyte infiltration into the median eminence may have a role in oestrous cycle maintenance, whereas Irf7 in tanycytes modulates circulating monocyte proportions, revealing brain–immune system communication through tanycytes. Our findings reveal an immune-associated role for tanycytes, with potential implications for understanding the endocrine and immunological mechanisms underlying sex-biased diseases.

title: Metabolic homeostasis and women’s reproductive health
abstract: Metabolic homeostasis and female reproductive health are governed by tightly coupled regulatory systems, yet their reciprocal interactions have often been investigated in isolation. In this Review, we synthesize current epidemiological, mechanistic and clinical evidence to propose an integrated framework in which dynamic, bidirectional crosstalk between key metabolic organs and endocrine mediators constitutes a central determinant of female reproductive function across the life course. We delineate how disruption of this integrated network underpins a broad spectrum of reproductive dysfunction, particularly in polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome and reproductive ageing, as well as cardiometabolic risk, highlighting the bidirectional nature of these associations. Finally, we critically evaluate current metabolism-targeted strategies, including lifestyle interventions, metabolic surgery and pharmacological therapies, and discuss emerging opportunities for precision approaches. By integrating mechanistic insights with clinical evidence, this Review reframes female reproductive disorders from a systemic metabolic perspective and outlines future directions for metabolism-focused strategies to improve reproductive health outcomes.

title: NNMT enhances hyperandrogenism in polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome through epigenetic remodelling
abstract: Polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome (PMOS) features intertwined reproductive, endocrine and metabolic defects, yet its initiating mechanisms remain incompletely understood. Here we show that an epigenetic mechanism driven by nicotinamide N -methyltransferase (NNMT) in granulosa cells contributes to disease progression in PMOS. We observe that Nnmt overexpression in mouse granulosa cells reduces histone H3 lysine 27 trimethylation (H3K27me3), leading to increased retinoic acid receptor beta (RARB) expression. RARB, in turn, amplifies ovarian androgen synthesis. The resulting androgen excess further suppresses H3K27me3, locking cells into a feedforward loop that sustains hyperandrogenism and disrupts follicle development. Pharmacological inhibition of NNMT restores H3K27me3, disrupts the RARB–androgen feedback circuit, and ameliorates both metabolic and hormonal phenotypes in PMOS models. Our findings suggest NNMT as a regulator of PMOS through metabolic and epigenetic reprogramming. The NNMT–H3K27me3–RARB–androgen axis emerges as a mechanistic nexus linking methionine and epigenetic dysregulation to PMOS pathogenesis and represents a tractable therapeutic target.

title: A futile Na+ K+ transport cycle augments energy expenditure in beige adipocytes
abstract: Uncoupling protein 1 (UCP1)-independent energy dissipation has been proven to serve physiological functions in beige adipocytes. Here we show that a futile sodium/potassium (Na + /K + ) transport cycle is preferentially amplified in mouse and human beige adipocytes and contributes to UCP1-independent energy expenditure. In mice, cold exposure activates a sympathetic–thyroid hormone signaling axis that coordinatedly induces the Na + /K + -ATPase subunit ATP1A2 together with Na + and K + channels, increasing bidirectional ion flux across the plasma membrane while maintaining ionic balance. Atp1a2 + Kcnk3 + adipocytes are detected in mouse inguinal white adipose tissue after cold exposure. Acute inhibition of Na + /K + -ATPase reduces energy expenditure in mouse and human beige adipocytes, whereas overexpressing Atp1a2 in murine adipocytes potentiates energy expenditure, independent of UCP1. Adipocyte-specific Atp1a2 deletion impairs thermogenic capacity and exacerbates diet-induced obesity in mice. Expression of a human ATP1A2 missense variant reduces ATP1A2-dependent respiration in mouse adipocytes. Together, these identify ion transport as a tunable ATP-consuming mechanism that expands the thermogenic repertoire of beige adipocytes.

title: Respiratory stress unmasks asparagine vulnerability
abstract: Cells can tolerate substantial mitochondrial stress through anaplerosis. Cui et al. identify pyruvate carboxylase as a key metabolic control point for asparagine auxotrophy that emerges with severe respiratory dysfunction.

title: Respiration-deficient cells require pyruvate carboxylase to suppress asparagine auxotrophy
abstract: Mutations in mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) impair ETC activity and oxidative phosphorylation, but their phenotypic consequences vary with heteroplasmy levels. Whether increasing mtDNA heteroplasmy creates metabolic dependencies not present in respiratory-competent cells remains unknown. Here, we show that low pyruvate carboxylase (PC) expression creates an asparagine dependency in high-mtDNA-heteroplasmy, respiration-compromised cells. In isogenic cells carrying similar mtDNA deletions, respiration declines linearly with increasing heteroplasmy, whereas redox imbalance emerges only above 50% heteroplasmy. Above 70% heteroplasmy, integrated stress-response-associated translational defects emerge, which can be reversed by either exogenous asparagine or PC overexpression. Asparagine dependence inversely correlates with PC expression across respiration-deficient cells. Consistent with this pattern, patient-derived thyroid tumour cells harbouring a high-heteroplasmy complex I mutation and low PC levels exhibit asparagine auxotrophy and sensitivity to L -asparaginase. Together, these findings demonstrate a role for mitochondrial PC in cellular asparagine synthesis under conditions of compromised respiratory activity.

Author Correction: Hypothalamic Grb10 enhances leptin signalling and promotes weight loss
Balancing de novo and salvage pathways in cellular nucleotide synthesis
abstract: Nucleotides are essential for DNA replication, repair and transcription and are supplied through two principal pathways, salvage and de novo synthesis. While the core enzymes underlying these pathways have long been characterized, recent work has uncovered mechanisms that regulate pathway choice across cell states. This Review summarizes our current understanding of how cells govern the balance between salvage and de novo synthesis of nucleotides. We examine context-dependent pathway utilization across organisms, tissues and physiological contexts, and discuss the molecular determinants of pathway choice, including precursor availability, cellular demand, transcriptional programmes, mitochondrial and one-carbon metabolism, post-translational regulation and multienzyme organization. We further explore how disruption of this balance shapes human disease and consider the translational potential of nucleotide metabolic plasticity. Finally, we highlight emerging technologies for resolving tissue-specific and cell-type-specific pathway utilization and outline outstanding questions in pathway regulation and therapeutic targeting. Collectively, this Review summarizes current knowledge of how cells dynamically balance de novo synthesis and salvage and highlights opportunities to therapeutically target nucleotide metabolic dependencies.

title: Whole-blood NAD levels track cardiovascular disease but not chronological age
abstract: The extent to which whole-blood NAD levels are altered in human disease or ageing remains controversial. Here we conducted 1,340 measurements in 1,068 adults, and found that whole-blood NAD levels do not decline with age in healthy individuals; they remain stable in males and increase in females, but are reduced in chronic diseases, specifically cardiovascular disease and hypertension. These findings indicate that whole-blood NAD levels track cardiovascular disease rather than chronological age. As this research was not designed to investigate causality, these data do not provide direct evidence that NAD supplementation may serve as a treatment for cardiovascular disease or hypertension.

title: The bleeding edge of NAD in human ageing
abstract: Whole-blood nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD) levels do not consistently decline with age, challenging the notion that lower systemic NAD levels cause age-related diseases. However, blood NAD levels provide an incomplete view of systemic NAD metabolism, failing to capture the heterogeneity of NAD metabolism across blood and solid tissues.
